questiontext.text: What is the central mechanism of the Rabin-Karp algorithm?

answer.text: A rolling hash that compares each length-m window's hash against the pattern's hash

feedback.text: Correct — hashing turns each window comparison into an O(1) check.

answer.text: A failure function that avoids text backtracking

feedback.text: No — that is KMP.

answer.text: Right-to-left comparison with a bad-character rule

feedback.text: No — that is Boyer-Moore.

answer.text: Sorting the text and binary searching

feedback.text: No — Rabin-Karp does not sort.

generalfeedback.text: Rabin-Karp hashes the pattern once, then slides a rolling hash over the text so each window's hash updates in O(1).

questiontext.text: Thanks to the rolling hash, how much work does Rabin-Karp do to update the window hash when it slides by one position?

answer.text: O(1) per step

feedback.text: Correct — the rolling hash removes the outgoing character and adds the incoming one in constant time.

answer.text: O(m) per step

feedback.text: No — recomputing from scratch would be O(m); the rolling hash avoids that.

answer.text: O(log m) per step

feedback.text: No — the update is constant time, not logarithmic.

answer.text: O(n) per step

feedback.text: No — each slide is O(1), not O(n).

generalfeedback.text: The rolling hash updates in O(1) by subtracting the leaving character's contribution and adding the entering character's.

answer.text: Average O(n + m), worst O(n × m)

feedback.text: Correct — worst case arises when hash collisions force verifying every window.

answer.text: Average O(n + m), worst O(n + m)

feedback.text: No — that is KMP; Rabin-Karp's worst case is O(nm) due to collisions.

answer.text: Average O(n/m), worst O(n × m)

feedback.text: No — sublinear average is Boyer-Moore, not Rabin-Karp.

answer.text: Average O(log n), worst O(n)

feedback.text: No — Rabin-Karp is linear on average, not logarithmic.

generalfeedback.text: Average O(n + m); worst O(nm) when many spurious hash hits force character-by-character verification.

questiontext.text: Rabin-Karp updates each window's fingerprint in O(1) using a ______ hash. Give the missing word.

answer.text: rolling

feedback.text: Correct — the rolling hash.

answer.text: rolling*

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: For which scenario is Rabin-Karp the most natural choice?

answer.text: Searching for many patterns of the same length at once (e.g. plagiarism/dedup detection)

feedback.text: Correct — one window hash can be tested against a whole set of pattern hashes.

answer.text: When you need a guaranteed worst-case linear single-pattern search

feedback.text: No — Rabin-Karp's worst case is O(nm); KMP gives the linear guarantee.

answer.text: When you want the largest average-case skips on a big alphabet

feedback.text: No — that is Boyer-Moore.

answer.text: When you must sort the text lexicographically

feedback.text: No — Rabin-Karp does not sort.

generalfeedback.text: Rabin-Karp's rolling hash makes checking a window against a set of pattern hashes cheap, so it excels at multi-pattern search.

questiontext.text: A hash match in Rabin-Karp must still be verified character-by-character, because two different strings can share the same hash (a spurious hit).

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — equal hashes do not guarantee equal strings, so verification is required.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: No — hash collisions mean a match must be confirmed by direct comparison.

questiontext.text: Rabin-Karp is especially well suited to searching for many patterns at once by comparing each window hash against a set of pattern hashes.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — multi-pattern search is Rabin-Karp's standout strength.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: No — checking one window hash against a set of hashes is exactly why Rabin-Karp shines for multiple patterns.

questiontext.text: Which statements about Rabin-Karp are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It excels at searching for multiple patterns simultaneously

feedback.text: Yes — compare each window hash against a set of pattern hashes.

answer.text: Its worst case is O(n × m) when hash collisions force many verifications

feedback.text: Yes — frequent spurious hits push it toward the naive bound.

answer.text: A hash match guarantees the strings are equal, so no verification is needed

feedback.text: No — collisions are possible, so matches must be verified.

answer.text: It guarantees O(n + m) worst-case time like KMP

feedback.text: No — its worst case is O(nm); only the average is O(n + m).

generalfeedback.text: Rabin-Karp: great for multiple patterns, average O(n + m), worst O(nm) from collisions, and every hash hit needs verification.
